entry.evidence: it is unknown if concentrated föhn jets spilled onto the former LAIS and LBIS and, if so, whether those föhn winds contributed to their collapse

steps.action: The authors take up the Massom et al. (2018) conceptual model of four prerequisites for rapid collapse (surface flooding and hydrofracture, reduced sea ice, terminus fracturing, calving trigger) as the frame for the collapse mechanism.
steps.quote: a conceptual model for rapid ice shelf collapse proposed by Massom et al. (2018) identifies four essential prerequisites for sudden collapse

steps.action: The authors cite field and satellite observations that clear skies and warm west-northwest föhn winds were present at the time of both collapses.
steps.quote: meteorological and satellite observations identify clear skies and warm west-northwest föhn wind at the time of collapse

steps.action: The authors pose three questions: the föhn share of the melt budget on each eastern AP ice shelf, whether föhn helped trigger the LAIS and LBIS collapses, and the implications for remaining shelves.
steps.quote: [...] öhn winds and associated melt play a role in triggering the collapses of the LAIS and LBIS?

steps.action: The authors take 3-hourly, 5.5 km RACMO2 v2.3p2 hindcast output for 1979-2018, curated by a co-author, as the reconstruction of past surface melt and meteorology, and cite earlier AWS evaluations of the model.
steps.quote: We base our analysis on 3-hourly output from simulations by the Regional Atmospheric Climate Model 2 (RACMO2), version 2.3p2

steps.action: The authors apply their earlier föhn detection algorithm (FöhnDA: AWS thresholds from quantile regression, T > 0 °C) and the machine learning model trained on it to detect föhn in RACMO2 output where no AWS exist.
steps.quote: the föhn detection algorithm (FöhnDA) that identifies föhn winds that cause melt using 12 automatic weather stations (AWSs) on the AP previously developed

steps.action: From wind direction and strength and from the föhn melt pattern in RACMO2, the authors establish seven recurring föhn jets, three of them (LA, LB, JP) new.
steps.quote: we identify seven recurring föhn jets or “gap winds” that lead to high surface melt rates on the eastern AP ice shelves

steps.action: The authors estimate the föhn-induced share of total melt and of melt hours per ice shelf for 1979-2002: 42 % on LAIS and 51 % on LBIS, against 25 % on SCAR inlet and 17 % on LCIS.
steps.quote: Föhn-induced surface melt accounts for 42 % of the total annual melt between 1979 and 2002 on the LAIS

steps.action: The authors contrast collapsed and intact shelves in föhn melt amount, fraction, and spatial reach, including whether the jets reach the calving front (Fig. 3b).
steps.quote: The stark contrast in surface melt amount and fraction caused by föhn winds on collapsed vs. intact ice shelves implicates föhn melt as a contributor

steps.action: From the RACMO2 melt time series (Fig. 4b), the authors find three föhn events on LAIS from 18 to 27 January 1995 that overlap the collapse onset dated by Rott et al. (1998).
steps.quote: Three föhn wind events occurred on LAIS between 18 and 27 January 1995, overlapping with the initial phase of the LAIS collapse

steps.action: The authors quantify the 9 d föhn melt (268.5 mm w.e., 25.2 % of the season's melt, the largest of any 9 d period in 1979-2018) and judge it anomalous.
steps.quote: produced increased surface melt greater than any other 9 d period from 1979–2018, with mean cumulative melt of 268.5 mm w.e.

steps.action: The authors correlate summer föhn hours with ERA5 sea ice concentration east of each shelf for 1979-2018, compare that correlation with the one for air temperature, and show the sea ice drop during the 1995 event (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: We also identify a negative correlation between the occurrence of föhn winds and sea ice concentration on all eastern AP ice shelves

steps.action: The authors estimate LAIS melt lake extent from an analogous 8 December 1992 AVHRR image (5.1-10.8 % of area) and lake depth from the RACMO2 liquid water of the 9 d event.
steps.quote: We find mean melt lake depth to be between 1.38–6.86 m depending on lake location and föhn influence

steps.action: The authors take Banwell et al. (2013)'s modelled lake depth of 5 m, the depth that can drive hydrofracture cascades, as the expectation to compare against.
steps.quote: the modeled lake depth (5 m) that could lead to large-scale hydrofracture cascades

steps.action: The authors compare the estimated LAIS lake depths with the observed LBIS pre-collapse mean depth (1 m) and the modelled critical depth (5 m).
steps.quote: [...] average lake depth of the LBIS lakes prior to collapse (1 m)

steps.action: The authors find föhn events in RACMO2 just before, at, and after the 9 February 2002 LBIS collapse onset, and quantify their melt rates (Fig. 4e).
steps.quote: A föhn wind event coincided with the initial LBIS collapse on 9 February 2002

steps.action: The authors propose that earlier high-melt föhn seasons preconditioned LBIS through firn densification, to be examined in Sect. 3.3.
steps.quote: previous high-melt-rate föhn events such as those in the 1992/1993 and 1994/1995 melt seasons likely preconditioned the LBIS through firn densification

steps.action: The authors use two-tailed t-tests of 1980-2002 shelf climatologies against LBIS: total melt differs across shelves, but with föhn melt removed SCAR inlet and Larsen C (north) are statistically indistinguishable from LBIS.
steps.quote: melt production on SCAR inlet and LCIS is statistically indistinguishable at the 95 % confidence interval from LBIS melt production

steps.action: The authors repeat the intercomparison with LAIS instead of LBIS as the reference shelf and report qualitatively similar results; this is reported in Methods only.
steps.quote: Qualitatively similar results are obtained when comparing all ice shelves to the LAIS.

steps.action: The authors compute the liquid-to-solid ratio (LSR) as a crude proxy for firn air content, with and without föhn-induced melt (Fig. 7).
steps.quote: The LSR for LAIS and LBIS is also just above 1 for this period, though only if föhn-induced surface melt is excluded

steps.action: The authors compare LSR between collapsed and intact shelves and conclude that föhn melt preconditioned LAIS and LBIS by long-term firn densification.
steps.quote: Thus the collapsed ice shelves experienced climatological LSRs significantly larger than the SCAR inlet and the LCIS

steps.action: The authors argue that the north-south temperature gradient alone, and suture-zone weakness alone (present on all shelves, while only two collapsed), do not explain why LAIS and LBIS stand out.
steps.quote: However, the temperature gradient alone does not explain the substantial increase in surface melt on the LAIS and LBIS relative to more southerly ice shelves

steps.action: To account for the absence of collapse in the high-melt 1992/1993 season, the authors invoke early-season timing with more buffering pore space (§4 ¶2) and misaligned Massom prerequisites, since sea ice was still at the front in the 1992 AVHRR image (§4 ¶3).
steps.quote: a possible misalignment of the four prerequisites for rapid collapse theorized by Massom et al. (2018)

steps.action: The authors keep the claim that föhn winds and föhn melt played a significant role in both collapses, and that extant shelves are unlikely to collapse from föhn melt in the current climate.
steps.quote: We conclude that föhn winds and the associated surface melt played a significant role in the collapses of the LAIS and LBIS

No; föhn melt on the vanished shelves is inferred from RACMO2 with an ML föhn detector

Partly: temperature gradient, suture zones, Massom prerequisites; basal melt set aside
Partly: removing föhn melt should make collapsed and intact shelves alike
Conditions found in past events, reconstructed by model and reanalysis

tree.answer: Two collapses plus intact shelves and a 40-year climatology act as nature's repeats
One robustness check (reference shelf); detector checks inherited
Kept as best explanation from converging lines of evidence

end.claim: Föhn winds and the associated surface melt played a significant role in the LAIS and LBIS collapses: they formed extensive melt lakes, preconditioned the firn, and pushed sea ice from the calving front. Extant eastern AP shelves are unlikely to collapse from föhn-induced melt in the current climate.

decisive_move.sentence: The föhn-induced melt share on the now-vanished Larsen A and B shelves, obtained by applying the AWS-trained föhn detector to RACMO2 output, is the quantity without which neither the shelf contrasts nor the collapse-timing argument would exist.

gates.evidence: All data are existing RACMO2 hindcast output, ERA5 reanalysis and archived satellite imagery (§2.1 ¶1, §2.4 ¶1); no acquisition was directed by a hypothesis. The non-föhn melt t-test (§3.3 ¶1) could have failed: collapsed shelves could have stayed distinct after föhn melt was removed. The coincidence and lake-depth arguments (§3.2) carry no stated failure criterion. No hypothesis, threshold or analysis is said to have been fixed before the data were examined; the 95 % significance level is a convention.

imports.item: Binary-classification machine learning model (scikit-learn) trained on AWS-based föhn labels and applied to model output
Quantile regression to set site-specific wind speed and relative humidity thresholds
Two-tailed t-test for differences in shelf climatologies
Pearson correlation between föhn occurrence and sea ice concentration

novelty_claims.quote: The remaining three jets (LA, LB, and JP) are, to our knowledge, identified here for the first time.
allows for new föhn jet identification on the LAIS and LBIS despite lack of direct observation
this research highlights a new understanding behind föhn melt mechanisms for ice shelf collapse

limits: Sub-claims and their statuses: (a) three newly identified föhn jets (LA, LB, JP), established in model output only, with no direct observation: regularity_in_range at best (§2.2 ¶2, §3.1 ¶1). (b) föhn caused about 25 % ± 3 % of annual melt in 9 d on LAIS: estimate_with_resolution, but the source of the ±3 % is not stated in the main text (§0 ¶1, §3.2.1 ¶1). (c) LAIS melt lake depth of 1.38-6.86 m: estimate_with_resolution resting on an analogue image from 1992 and assumed lake areas (§3.2.1 ¶2). (d) SCAR inlet and LCIS unlikely to collapse from föhn melt: conditional projection with status none, not tested (§5 ¶2). Process gaps: the ML föhn detector and its validation (the >23 % accuracy gain and the sensitivity study) appear to come from Laffin et al. (2021); whether any of this was redone here is unclear (inference). The RACMO2 evaluation against AWS is cited, not performed. No uncertainty propagation from the detector or the model into the föhn melt fractions is reported. Basal melting and ocean forcing are explicitly not considered (§4 ¶4). The paper went through open discussion and two anonymous referees (PDF p. 11), but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded and the origin of checks such as the LAIS reference-shelf test (§2.3 ¶1) cannot be attributed to review. Causal language ('helped contribute', 'played a significant role') rests on coincidence in time and contrasts between shelves, not on a counterfactual simulation without föhn.

disagreements.target: Massom et al. (2018) conceptual model of collapse triggered by sea ice loss and ocean swell
disagreements.support: RACMO2 föhn timing and the ERA5 sea ice correlation are used to argue that föhn winds produced both the melt lakes and the sea ice clearance that the Massom model treats as separate prerequisites.
disagreements.quote: the off-coast wind direction created by föhn winds helped melt and physically push sea ice away from the ice shelf calving fronts

disagreements.target: Studies proposing suture zones as a major contributor to instability (Glasser and Scambos, 2008; Borstad et al., 2016)
disagreements.support: All shelves in the region are sutured, yet only two collapsed, so suture zones cannot by themselves account for which shelves failed.
disagreements.quote: while some studies suggest this is a major contributor to ice shelf instability, only two of the ice shelves have collapsed

disagreements.target: Explanation of collapse by the north-south temperature gradient and warming (Scambos et al., 2003; Morris [...] )
disagreements.support: With föhn melt removed, melt on SCAR inlet and Larsen C (north) is statistically indistinguishable from LBIS, so temperature alone does not single out the collapsed shelves.

alternatives_considered.chosen: LBIS as the reference shelf for the t-test intercomparison
alternatives_considered.reason: LBIS was the most recent collapse and is adjacent to both collapsed and existing ice shelves

alternatives_considered.chosen: ML model trained on FöhnDA labels to detect föhn in RACMO2 output
alternatives_considered.alternatives: simple binary classification method applied to RACMO2 output
alternatives_considered.reason: accuracy of föhn detection improves by over 23 %

alternatives_considered.alternatives: previous föhn detection methods (Cape et al., 2015; Datta et al., 2019)
alternatives_considered.reason: it allows AWS observations to extend föhn detection to regions and times without AWS (sensitivity study in Laffin et al., 2021; Fig. S1, Table S1)

alternatives_considered.chosen: AVHRR image of 8 December 1992 as an analogue for LAIS melt lake extent
alternatives_considered.alternatives: satellite imagery taken during the 1995 collapse (Fig. S3)
alternatives_considered.reason: many lakes had likely drained or been altered once collapse had begun, so extent cannot be estimated from those images

alternatives_considered.chosen: föhn wind occurrence as the driver of reduced sea ice concentration
alternatives_considered.reason: sea ice concentration is more strongly correlated with föhn occurrence than with air temperature (Fig. 5a, b)
